Soever
so-ev'er
adv. (a generalizing particle, standing apart from its pronoun in the Authorized Version: what man soever, what thing soever — the 1611 way of saying “any… at all”)
A compound of so and ever. In 1611 English the particle could stand detached from its interrogative — what man soever rather than whatsoever man — and the Authorized translators kept the separated form where the Hebrew put a word between. It renders the Hebrew ish ish, “a man, a man,” a doubling that means any man whatever.

Biblical Definition

The separated soever is one of the surest marks of the Authorized Version's age, and it is not a mannerism — it is following the Hebrew. The idiom ish ish, literally “a man, a man,” is Hebrew for any man at all, and the translators reproduced its structure: “What man soever there be of the house of Israel, that killeth an ox, or lamb, or goat, in the camp, or that killeth it out of the camp” (Leviticus 17:3). The same construction covers the priesthood: “What man soever of the seed of Aaron is a leper, or hath a running issue; he shall not eat of the holy things, until he be clean” (Leviticus 22:4) — the holiness of the office gave no exemption from the law of cleanness. Hushai uses it of intelligence to be passed to David: “what thing soever thou shalt hear out of the king's house, thou shalt tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests” (2 Samuel 15:35). And Moses uses it to close the law against tampering: “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32). In each case the particle does one job — it removes every exception.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines soever as a word chiefly used in composition with who, what, where and how, and notes that it may be separated from these by an intervening word.

expand to see more

SOEVER, a word compounded of so and ever, and annexed to who, what, where, how, as, whosoever, whatsoever, wheresoever, howsoever.

It may be separated from the pronoun or adverb by the intervening word; as, what man soever; how great soever.

WHOSOEVER, pron. Any person whatever.

WHATSOEVER, pron. Whatever; any thing that; being of any nature, kind or sort.

EVER, adv. At any time; at any period or point of time.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 12:32 — "What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it."

Leviticus 17:3 — "What man soever there be of the house of Israel, that killeth an ox, or lamb, or goat, in the camp, or that killeth it out of the camp,"

Leviticus 22:4 — "What man soever of the seed of Aaron is a leper, or hath a running issue; he shall not eat of the holy things, until he be clean. And whoso toucheth any thing that is unclean by the dead, or a man whose seed goeth from him;"

2 Samuel 15:35 — "And hast thou not there with thee Zadok and Abiathar the priests? therefore it shall be, that what thing soever thou shalt hear out of the king's house, thou shalt tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests."

Modern Corruption

The Authorized Version's archaisms are treated as obstacles to be smoothed away, when several of them — this one included — are the translators reproducing the shape of the original.

expand to see more

It is often assumed that the Authorized Version's odd constructions are seventeenth-century English being quaint, and that a modern rendering loses nothing by regularising them. What man soever is a case where the assumption fails. The Hebrew ish ish is a doubling for emphasis, and the separated particle is the translators' attempt to let an English reader see that something is being doubled. Their preface, The Translators to the Reader, explains the policy at length: they aimed at a version transparent to the original, not at an elegant English composition, and they were willing to write awkward English to do it. The italics marking supplied words come from the same conviction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the particle is doing theologically, which is the removal of exceptions. Leviticus 22:4 is the sharpest instance: what man soever of the seed of Aaron — priestly descent conferred privilege and conferred no immunity, and a leprous priest ate no holy thing until he was clean. Deuteronomy 12:32 does the same for the law as a whole: not most things, not the important things, but what thing soever I command you. The old word is doing the work that the phrase without exception does now, and it is worth pausing over rather than translating past.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ish ish, “a man, a man” — the doubling behind what man soever, Leviticus 17:3, 22:4; kol ha-dabar, the whole word or thing — Deuteronomy 12:32.

expand to see more

Hebrew ish ish — literally “a man, a man”; the emphatic doubling meaning any man whatever.

Hebrew kol — all, every, the whole; the generalizing word behind many of these constructions.

Hebrew dabar — a word or thing; Deuteronomy 12:32, “what thing soever.”

Greek hosos — as much as, whatsoever; the New Testament equivalent construction.

English so + ever; in 1611 the particle could stand apart from its pronoun.

Usage

"“What man soever” — the Hebrew doubling ish ish, reproduced in English."

"“What man soever of the seed of Aaron” — priestly descent bought no exemption."

"“What thing soever I command you” — the particle exists to remove exceptions."
